options.a: Drain, waste, and vent
options.b: Drain, water, and valve
options.c: Domestic water and vent
options.d: Direct waste ventilation

distractorExplanations.b: Swaps waste and vent for water and valve; DWV is the sanitary drainage side, not supply valves.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes in domestic water, which is the supply side; DWV is the drainage system kept separate from potable piping.
distractorExplanations.d: Not a code term; in DWV the D stands for drain and the V for the vent piping that protects trap seals.

options.a: 1/8 inch per foot for 3 inch and smaller; 1/16 inch per foot for 4 inch and larger
options.b: 1/4 inch per foot for 3 inch and smaller; 1/8 inch per foot for 4 inch and larger
options.c: 1/2 inch per foot for 3 inch and smaller; 1/4 inch per foot for 4 inch and larger
options.d: 1 inch per foot for 3 inch and smaller; 1/2 inch per foot for 4 inch and larger

distractorExplanations.a: Halves both values; 1/16 in/ft applies only to 8-inch and larger drains, and small drains need more than 1/8 in/ft.
distractorExplanations.c: Doubles both values; 1/2 in/ft is steeper than the tabulated minimum and is not the code requirement for small drains.
distractorExplanations.d: Far steeper than the code minimum; excessive slope is not required and can let liquids outrun solids in the drain.

options.a: Pressurize drain lines to speed up flow
options.b: Provide an overflow path for wastewater during a stoppage
options.c: Protect trap seals and allow air into drainage system
options.d: Prevent cross-connections between potable supply and drain lines

distractorExplanations.a: Vents equalize drains to atmospheric pressure; positive pressure in drains would blow out trap seals rather than help flow.
distractorExplanations.b: Dry vents carry air, not wastewater; using a vent as a backup drain path during a clog is a code violation.
distractorExplanations.d: Cross-connection protection is the job of air gaps and backflow preventers on the supply side, not DWV vents.

options.a: 1/2 inch minimum, 1 inch maximum
options.b: 1 inch minimum (varies by code)
options.c: 1-1/2 inches minimum per fixture type
options.d: 2 inches minimum (varies by code)

distractorExplanations.a: Far too shallow; a 1/2-inch seal is lost quickly to evaporation or siphonage. Codes require 2 in minimum and 4 in maximum.
distractorExplanations.b: 1 inch is half the code minimum; trap seal depth must be at least 2 inches and not more than 4 inches.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the common 1-1/2 inch trap pipe size with seal depth; the required seal depth is 2 inches minimum.

options.a: One pipe to serve as drain and vent for multiple fixtures
options.b: One vent to serve two fixture drains joined at the same level
options.c: A storm drain to double as the vent for a sanitary branch
options.d: An air admittance valve to serve in place of every vent stack

distractorExplanations.b: That describes a common (dual) vent, which carries no waste; a wet vent also receives drainage from other fixtures.
distractorExplanations.c: Storm and sanitary systems must stay separate; a storm conductor cannot serve as the vent for sanitary fixtures.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses wet venting with AAVs; AAVs are mechanical devices and codes still require at least one open vent to outdoors.

options.a: Access for pressure testing at each fixture trap before final inspection
options.b: Access for rodding drainage system at changes of direction and intervals
options.c: Access to vent piping at each roof penetration for clearing frost closure
options.d: Access to water supply shutoffs at each fixture group for maintenance

distractorExplanations.a: Test tees and plugs serve testing; code cleanouts exist for rodding stoppages at direction changes and set spacing.
distractorExplanations.c: Vent terminals are not cleanout locations; cleanouts go on the drainage system at direction changes and intervals.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses cleanouts with supply shutoff access; cleanouts are DWV fittings for rodding, not potable valve access.

options.a: Allows the building to omit the vent stack through the roof
options.b: Releases sewer gas when positive pressure builds in the drain
options.c: Admits air when drainage draws vacuum; seals when not needed
options.d: Lets air out of the water supply to prevent water hammer

distractorExplanations.a: Codes still require at least one vent extending to open air for each building drain; AAVs supplement, not replace, the stack.
distractorExplanations.b: AAVs are one-way: they open only on negative pressure and seal against positive pressure, so they do not relieve it.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an AAV with an air chamber or water hammer arrestor on the supply side; AAVs are DWV vent devices.

options.a: Building sewer to the public main at the property line
options.b: Vent stacks to the roof terminal above the top floor
options.c: Fixture traps directly to the stack on each floor
options.d: Branch drains to building sewer outside foundation

distractorExplanations.a: That is the building sewer's run; the building drain is the lowest piping inside the structure that feeds the sewer.
distractorExplanations.b: Vent stacks carry air to the roof; the building drain is the horizontal drainage collector at the lowest level.
distractorExplanations.c: Fixture arms and branches tie fixtures to stacks; the building drain collects the stacks and branches at the base.

options.a: They can lose seal by siphonage without venting
options.b: They trap debris and cause frequent stoppages
options.c: Their seal is too deep to drain quickly
options.d: They exceed the maximum trap arm length

distractorExplanations.b: S-traps are banned because they siphon their own seal, not because they clog more often than a P-trap.
distractorExplanations.c: Seal depth is not the defect; S-traps lose their seal by self-siphonage because the outlet drops without a vent.
distractorExplanations.d: Trap arm length is a separate vent-distance rule; the S-trap's problem is the vertical drop that siphons the seal.

options.a: Based on IPC/UPC drain sizing tables (~10 FU for 3" at 1/4"/ft slope)
options.b: Based on IPC/UPC drain sizing tables (~42 FU for 3" at 1/4"/ft slope)
options.c: Based on IPC/UPC drain sizing tables (~84 FU for 3" at 1/4"/ft slope)
options.d: Based on IPC/UPC drain sizing tables (~216 FU for 3" at 1/4"/ft slope)

distractorExplanations.a: Far too low; a 3-inch drain at 1/4 in/ft carries roughly 42 dfu in the IPC building-drain table, not about 10.
distractorExplanations.c: Doubles the tabulated value; about 84 dfu would overload a 3-inch drain, so higher loads call for a 4-inch drain.
distractorExplanations.d: About 216 dfu is the IPC value for a 4-inch building drain at 1/4 in/ft; it does not apply to a 3-inch pipe.

options.a: Inside a ventilated attic space above the ceiling insulation line
options.b: Under a roof overhang next to soffit intake vents
options.c: Open to outdoor air, typically through roof with proper clearance
options.d: Through a sidewall directly below an operable window

distractorExplanations.a: Vents must extend to open air outside; ending in an attic, even a ventilated one, releases sewer gas into the building.
distractorExplanations.b: Codes prohibit vent terminals beneath overhangs with soffit vents because sewer gas is drawn back into the attic.
distractorExplanations.d: Vent terminals may not sit directly beneath an openable window; IPC requires 10 ft horizontal or 3 ft above it.

options.a: Back-siphonage of potable water into the street main
options.b: Trap seal loss from induced siphonage
options.c: Normal flow of wastewater from fixtures to the sewer
options.d: Reverse flow of wastewater into fixtures

distractorExplanations.a: That is backflow in the potable supply context; in DWV, backflow means wastewater moving back into fixtures.
distractorExplanations.b: That is induced siphonage, a venting problem that empties traps, not wastewater flowing backward into fixtures.
distractorExplanations.c: That is ordinary forward drainage; backflow is flow in the reverse direction, toward and out of the fixtures.

options.a: CI is durable/quiet; PVC is lightweight with solvent weld joints
options.b: PVC is quieter; CI is lighter and joined with solvent cement
options.c: PVC is rated for higher heat; CI is limited to vent piping
options.d: CI is joined with solvent cement; PVC uses lead and oakum

distractorExplanations.b: Swaps the properties: cast iron is heavy and quieter, while PVC is light, noisier, and solvent-welded.
distractorExplanations.c: Cast iron tolerates heat better and is used for drains, not just vents; PVC has the lower temperature rating.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the joining methods: lead-and-oakum or no-hub couplings join CI, while PVC uses primer and solvent cement.

options.a: Left in the cleanout permanently to block sewer gas
options.b: Used to pressure-test the water supply before meter set
options.c: Used to air or water test system before concealment
options.d: Installed at the vent terminal to keep rain out of the stack

distractorExplanations.a: Test plugs are removed after testing; cleanouts are sealed with listed threaded plugs, not test balls left in place.
distractorExplanations.b: DWV test plugs seal drain openings; supply piping is tested with caps at working pressure, which is a different test.
distractorExplanations.d: Vent terminals must stay open after testing; a plug at the roof would block venting and siphon trap seals.

options.a: Air trapped in the vent stack after heavy drainage flow
options.b: Oversized supply piping that lowers water velocity
options.c: Thermal expansion from the water heater in a closed system
options.d: Sudden valve closure creating pressure surge in piping

distractorExplanations.a: Vent air affects DWV traps, not supply piping; water hammer is a supply-side pressure surge from rapid shutoff.
distractorExplanations.b: Larger pipe lowers velocity and reduces hammer; high velocity in undersized pipe plus quick closure causes it.
distractorExplanations.c: Thermal expansion raises static pressure gradually and is handled by an expansion tank; hammer is a sudden shock wave.

options.a: Potable supply from contamination due to cross-connection
options.b: Building drains from sewage backing up from the public sewer
options.c: Water heater from excess pressure due to thermal expansion
options.d: Fixtures from water hammer caused by quick-closing valves

distractorExplanations.b: Sewer backup into drains is addressed by backwater valves, not by backflow preventers on the domestic water service.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the role of the thermal expansion tank and T&P relief valve, not a backflow preventer on the service.
distractorExplanations.d: Water hammer arrestors handle pressure surges; a backflow preventer stops contaminated water reversing into potable.

options.a: Type M has thicker wall than Type L
options.b: Type L has thicker wall than Type M
options.c: Type L is red-coded; Type M is blue-coded
options.d: Type L has a larger outside diameter than M

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the order: wall thickness runs K (thickest), then L, then M (thinnest), so M is thinner than L.
distractorExplanations.c: Color codes are swapped: Type L is printed in blue and Type M in red, while Type K is marked in green.
distractorExplanations.d: Copper tube types share the same OD for each nominal size; only the wall thickness, and thus the ID, differs.

options.a: UV resistance for exposed outdoor runs in direct sunlight on roofs
options.b: Approval for DWV piping and solvent-welded drain fittings
options.c: Flexibility, corrosion resistance, and fewer fittings in some layouts
options.d: Higher rigidity, sweat-soldered joints, and wider support spacing

distractorExplanations.a: PEX degrades under UV exposure and must be shielded from sunlight; UV resistance is a weakness, not an advantage.
distractorExplanations.b: PEX is a pressure water distribution material; DWV uses PVC/ABS/cast iron, and PEX cannot be solvent-welded.
distractorExplanations.d: PEX is flexible, uses crimp or expansion fittings rather than solder, and needs closer support spacing than copper.

options.a: Excessive pressure from heated water with closed system
options.b: Water hammer when quick-closing fixture valves shut suddenly
options.c: Scalding at fixtures from stored water above 120°F
options.d: Sediment buildup at the bottom of the tank

distractorExplanations.b: Water hammer is a shock wave handled by arrestors; an expansion tank absorbs the slow volume growth from heating.
distractorExplanations.c: Scald protection comes from mixing valves or thermostat settings; expansion tanks do not limit water temperature.
distractorExplanations.d: Sediment is controlled by flushing the tank through its drain valve; an expansion tank has no effect on scale.

options.a: Bond copper to steel to improve electrical grounding continuity
options.b: Separate dissimilar metals to reduce galvanic corrosion
options.c: Join PEX to copper without a crimp or expansion fitting
options.d: Absorb vibration where piping connects to a pump

distractorExplanations.a: Opposite purpose: a dielectric union breaks the electrical path between metals; grounding continuity uses bonding jumpers.
distractorExplanations.c: PEX-to-copper transitions use listed adapters; dielectric unions isolate dissimilar metals such as copper and steel.
distractorExplanations.d: Vibration isolation uses flexible connectors; a dielectric union's purpose is electrical isolation against corrosion.

options.a: At the footing depth of the foundation
options.b: 12 inches deep in all cold-climate areas
options.c: Below frost line per local code
options.d: Above frost line with pipe insulation

distractorExplanations.a: Footing depth often relates to frost but is not the water-service rule; the pipe must sit below the local frost line.
distractorExplanations.b: 12 inches is a common minimum cover for building sewers, not a frost-protection depth for water service in cold climates.
distractorExplanations.d: Insulation alone does not stop buried service pipe from freezing; code requires burial below the frost line.

options.a: Water hammer from rapid valve closure in the shower
options.b: Backflow of shower water into the potable supply
options.c: Legionella growth in the storage water heater
options.d: Scalding from pressure/temperature fluctuations

distractorExplanations.a: Hammer arrestors address surges; pressure-balancing valves keep outlet temperature steady when supply pressure changes.
distractorExplanations.b: Backflow is stopped by check valves or vacuum breakers; mixing valves address the temperature swings that scald.
distractorExplanations.c: Legionella is controlled by storing hot water hot; the mixing valve's job is to prevent scalding at the outlet.

options.a: At service entrance to measure usage
options.b: At the water heater outlet to measure hot usage
options.c: After the pressure-reducing valve inside
options.d: At each fixture branch to bill per fixture

distractorExplanations.b: Some buildings submeter hot water, but the utility meter goes on the service line where water enters the property.
distractorExplanations.c: The meter sits at the service connection upstream of the building; a PRV is installed downstream of the meter.
distractorExplanations.d: Utility billing uses one service meter at the entrance; branch-level metering is not the typical meter location.

options.a: Raises water heater recovery rate on high demand
options.b: Reduces wait time by circulating hot water loop
options.c: Increases cold water pressure at distant fixtures
options.d: Mixes cold into the hot loop to prevent scalding

distractorExplanations.a: Recovery rate depends on burner or element input; a recirculation pump only moves already-heated water around the loop.
distractorExplanations.c: Recirculation pumps serve the hot water loop to cut wait time; they do not boost cold supply pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: Anti-scald protection comes from mixing valves; the pump circulates hot water so it reaches fixtures faster.

options.a: Flux applied after heating so it does not burn off
options.b: Solder melted by the flame onto an unheated, unfluxed joint
options.c: Clean, fluxed fittings heated until solder wicks into joint
options.d: Lead-bearing 50/50 solder for potable water lines

distractorExplanations.a: Flux goes on cleaned surfaces before heating; applying it after heating defeats its cleaning and wetting role.
distractorExplanations.b: The fitting must be cleaned, fluxed, and heated so solder melts on contact and wicks in; cold metal will not bond.
distractorExplanations.d: Since 1986, solder for potable lines must be lead-free (0.2% lead max); 50/50 tin-lead is prohibited there.

options.a: Add calcium to buffer acidic well water
options.b: Disinfect water with chlorine from the brine tank
options.c: Filter sediment through an activated carbon bed
options.d: Replace hardness ions with sodium/potassium

distractorExplanations.a: Calcite neutralizers add calcium to raise pH; softeners remove calcium and magnesium by ion exchange.
distractorExplanations.b: The brine tank holds salt to regenerate the resin; softeners do not disinfect, which is a separate chlorination step.
distractorExplanations.c: Carbon filters remove taste, odor, and chlorine; ion-exchange softening swaps calcium and magnesium for sodium.

options.a: Equipment drains that must not connect directly to sanitary
options.b: Fixtures that discharge directly through a trap to the stack
options.c: Storm water from roof drains and area drains
options.d: Sewage ejector pits that pump to the building drain

distractorExplanations.b: That is a direct connection; indirect waste receptors receive drains that must discharge through an air gap or air break.
distractorExplanations.c: Storm drainage goes to the storm system; indirect waste receptors take equipment drains such as ice machines.
distractorExplanations.d: Ejectors lift sewage from below sewer level and connect directly; indirect receptors take equipment and appliance drains.

options.a: 1.6 gpm at 60 psi
options.b: 2.5 gpm at 80 psi
options.c: 3.5 gpm at 80 psi
options.d: 4.0 gpm at 100 psi

distractorExplanations.a: 1.6 is the federal gallons-per-flush limit for toilets, not the showerhead flow cap of 2.5 gpm at 80 psi.
distractorExplanations.c: 3.5 gpm reflects older pre-1992 showerheads; EPAct 1992 capped showerhead flow at 2.5 gpm at 80 psi.
distractorExplanations.d: Far above the federal cap; 2.5 gpm at 80 psi has been the showerhead limit since the Energy Policy Act of 1992.

options.a: 12 inches from the stud face to the front edge of the closet flange
options.b: 12 inches from the stud wall to the flange's back edge
options.c: 12 inches from finished wall to center of closet flange
options.d: 15 inches from finished wall to center of the closet flange

distractorExplanations.a: Rough-in is measured from the finished wall surface to the flange center, not from the studs to the flange edge.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses the wrong reference points; the standard rough-in runs from the finished wall to the center of the flange.
distractorExplanations.d: 15 inches is the minimum side clearance from a toilet's centerline to a wall, not the rear-wall rough-in.

options.a: Accessible shutoff valves and S-trap with proper height
options.b: Concealed shutoff valves inside the wall with a drum trap
options.c: A single shutoff at the water heater and a crown-vented trap
options.d: Accessible shutoff valves and P-trap with proper height

distractorExplanations.a: S-traps are prohibited in new work because they self-siphon; lavatories require a vented P-trap.
distractorExplanations.b: Stops must stay accessible, and drum traps are generally prohibited for lavatories; a P-trap is required.
distractorExplanations.c: Each fixture needs its own accessible stops, and crown venting (a vent at the trap weir) is prohibited.

options.a: High loop or air gap before connection to drain/garbage disposal
options.b: A direct connection to the tailpiece below the trap weir
options.c: A check valve on the supply line at the dishwasher water inlet
options.d: A vacuum breaker on the drain hose at the disposal inlet

distractorExplanations.b: Connecting downstream of the trap bypasses the seal and admits sewer gas; the hose joins above the trap with a loop or air gap.
distractorExplanations.c: A supply check valve does not protect the drain hose; the drain needs a high loop or air gap to stop waste backflow.
distractorExplanations.d: Vacuum breakers protect potable supply lines; dishwasher drain hoses rely on an air gap or high loop instead.

options.a: Vents the floor drain trap to prevent siphonage
options.b: Maintains trap seal in seldom-used drains by adding water
options.c: Prevents sewer backup into the floor with a backwater flap
options.d: Removes debris from the trap by flushing on a timer

distractorExplanations.a: A primer adds water to replace evaporation; venting addresses siphonage, not evaporation in rarely used drains.
distractorExplanations.c: That is a backwater valve; a trap primer feeds small amounts of water to keep the trap seal from evaporating.
distractorExplanations.d: Primers deliver small makeup-water amounts to offset evaporation; they are not designed to flush debris out.

options.a: May rely on cement backer board as the waterproof layer
options.b: Is applied over the tile as a sealer coat
options.c: Must be waterproof before tile installation
options.d: Must be flood-tested only after grouting the tile

distractorExplanations.a: Cement board is not waterproof; a liner or membrane must be installed beneath or on it before tile is set.
distractorExplanations.b: The pan or liner goes under the mortar bed and tile; a topical sealer over finished tile is not a code shower pan.
distractorExplanations.d: The pan is flood-tested before tile so leaks can be fixed; testing after grouting means tearing out finished tile.

options.a: A dedicated vent separate from the sink's trap and vent
options.b: A hot-water supply connection to soften food waste
options.c: A direct connection to the building drain without a trap
options.d: Electrical connection and drain tie-in with proper trap/vent

distractorExplanations.a: A disposal discharges through the sink's own trap and vent; it does not need a separate dedicated vent.
distractorExplanations.b: Disposals take no water supply connection; manufacturers advise running cold water so fats solidify and flush.
distractorExplanations.c: Every fixture drain needs a trap; a disposal connects to the sink trap and cannot bypass it to the building drain.

options.a: Hot/cold supply and GFCI-protected electrical outlet nearby
options.b: A dedicated vent stack and its own 3-inch trap
options.c: A tee off the toilet supply with no vacuum breaker
options.d: A hardwired 240-volt circuit installed without GFCI protection

distractorExplanations.b: A bidet uses a small 1-1/4 inch trap tied into normal venting; it does not need its own stack or a 3-inch trap.
distractorExplanations.c: Bidet sprays create back-siphonage risk; codes require backflow protection such as an air gap or vacuum breaker.
distractorExplanations.d: Electric bidet seats plug into a 120 V receptacle that needs GFCI protection in a bathroom, not a 240 V circuit.

options.a: Floor-mounted water closets on a cast iron closet bend
options.b: Wall-hung fixtures like lavatories and water closets
options.c: Horizontal drain piping hung from the floor joists above
options.d: Water heaters mounted on a platform above the floor

distractorExplanations.a: Floor-mount toilets bolt to the closet flange; carriers hold wall-hung fixtures off the floor from inside the wall.
distractorExplanations.c: Pipe hangers and straps support horizontal drains; a carrier is a frame that anchors wall-hung fixtures.
distractorExplanations.d: Water heater stands are not carriers; carriers anchor wall-hung lavatories, urinals, and water closets.

options.a: Minimum handle rotation to keep water above 120°F
options.b: Maximum flow rate to keep showers under 2.5 gpm
options.c: Maximum handle rotation to cap hot water temperature
options.d: Water heater thermostat setting for the whole house

distractorExplanations.a: Limit stops cap the maximum hot rotation to prevent scalding; they do not set a minimum outlet temperature.
distractorExplanations.b: Flow is limited by the showerhead's restrictor; the limit stop restricts how far the handle turns toward hot.
distractorExplanations.d: The heater thermostat sets storage temperature; a limit stop caps outlet temperature at one valve only.

options.a: Adhesive anchors set in drywall without blocking
options.b: Rough-in set after tile so the spout height can be adjusted
options.c: A deck-mount valve body installed in the sink's back ledge
options.d: Correct rough-in dimensions and solid backing/blocking in wall

distractorExplanations.a: Drywall cannot carry faucet loads; wall-mount faucets need solid blocking behind and the correct rough-in.
distractorExplanations.b: Wall-mount rough-in must be set before tile and wall close; it cannot be adjusted after finishes are installed.
distractorExplanations.c: A deck-mount body is a different faucet type; wall-mount faucets need an in-wall valve body with backing.

options.a: High-pressure water from flush valve to cleanse fixture
options.b: A gravity tank that refills by float valve after each flush
options.c: Waterless cartridges that seal with a liquid barrier
options.d: Compressed air from the building system to scour the bowl

distractorExplanations.b: Gravity tanks are residential water closet systems; flushometers use line pressure delivered through a flush valve.
distractorExplanations.c: Waterless urinals use cartridges and no water; flushometer urinals deliver a pressurized water flush.
distractorExplanations.d: Pressure-assist toilets use air in a tank; flushometer urinals rely on supply water pressure through the valve.

options.a: A floor drain with trap primer under the washer
options.b: Recessed supply boxes with shutoffs and drain connection
options.c: A surface-mounted air gap fitting for the washer discharge hose
options.d: A dryer vent connection fitted with a backdraft damper

distractorExplanations.a: A floor pan or drain is optional protection; the washer box recesses the hot/cold valves and the standpipe drain.
distractorExplanations.c: Washers discharge into a standpipe via an air break; the box is a recess for shutoffs and the drain opening.
distractorExplanations.d: Dryer vent boxes are a separate item; the washing machine box houses supply valves and the standpipe drain.

options.a: Pedestal sinks with the rim at 36 inches maximum
options.b: Twist-knob faucets and a rim height of 38 inches
options.c: Clear knee space, height limits, and lever handles
options.d: Exposed drain pipes left uninsulated for inspection

distractorExplanations.a: ADA limits lavatory rim height to 34 inches and requires knee clearance, which pedestal bases block.
distractorExplanations.b: ADA requires controls operable without tight grasping or twisting and a rim no higher than 34 inches.
distractorExplanations.d: ADA requires hot water and drain pipes under accessible lavatories to be insulated or shielded to protect knees.

options.a: Uses a heat-trace cable to keep the valve warm
options.b: Contains an antifreeze reservoir in the valve body
options.c: Keeps water pressurized in the barrel to resist ice
options.d: Shuts water inside heated space to prevent freezing

distractorExplanations.a: Frost-free sillcocks need no heat trace; the long stem places the valve seat inside the heated wall cavity.
distractorExplanations.b: There is no antifreeze; the valve seat sits inside the building and the barrel drains when the valve is shut.
distractorExplanations.c: Pressurized water in the barrel would freeze; frost-free designs drain the barrel so no water stays outside.

options.a: Before walls close to verify layout, slope, and connections
options.b: After fixtures are set to verify flow and drainage
options.c: After drywall but before tile to check pipe supports
options.d: Before underground piping is installed to verify trench depth

distractorExplanations.b: That is the final inspection; rough-in inspection happens before walls close while the piping is exposed.
distractorExplanations.c: Supports and joints must be visible; once drywall is up the piping is concealed and rough-in cannot be verified.
distractorExplanations.d: Underground inspection is a separate, earlier step on installed buried pipe; rough-in covers above-ground piping.

options.a: ICC (International Code Council), which also publishes the IPC
options.b: NFPA (National Fire Protection Association), publisher of NFPA 54
options.c: IAPMO (International Association of Plumbing and Mechanical Officials)
options.d: ASME (American Society of Mechanical Engineers) via A112 standards

distractorExplanations.a: ICC publishes the International Plumbing Code (IPC); the Uniform Plumbing Code is IAPMO's model code.
distractorExplanations.b: NFPA publishes fire and fuel-gas codes such as NFPA 54 and NFPA 13; it does not publish the Uniform Plumbing Code.
distractorExplanations.d: ASME A112 covers plumbing fixture and fitting standards; ASME does not publish the UPC model code.

options.a: The model code publisher that writes the code text
options.b: The general contractor responsible for the whole project
options.c: The product listing agency that certifies fixtures
options.d: Local official/office enforcing code and issuing permits

distractorExplanations.a: ICC and IAPMO write model codes but have no enforcement power; the AHJ is the local enforcing official or office.
distractorExplanations.b: Contractors must comply with the code; the AHJ is the government official or office that enforces it.
distractorExplanations.c: Listing agencies such as UL or IAPMO R&T certify products; the AHJ decides approval and enforces the code.

options.a: Ensures code compliance and inspection for public health/safety
options.b: Transfers liability for any defects from the plumber to the city
options.c: Registers the installed fixtures for manufacturer warranty
options.d: Records the job for property tax reassessment purposes

distractorExplanations.b: A permit does not shift liability to the jurisdiction; it triggers inspections that verify code compliance.
distractorExplanations.c: Warranties are registered with manufacturers; permits exist so the AHJ can inspect work for health and safety.
distractorExplanations.d: Assessors may see permit data, but the code purpose of a plumbing permit is inspection for public health.

options.a: Prevent sewer gas from entering occupied spaces
options.b: Prevent potable water contamination
options.c: Keep stormwater out of sanitary sewers
options.d: Reduce water main pressure surges

distractorExplanations.a: Sewer gas is controlled by traps and vents; cross-connection control protects the potable supply from backflow.
distractorExplanations.c: Inflow and infiltration programs address stormwater in sewers; cross-connection control protects drinking water.
distractorExplanations.d: Surge control is a hydraulics issue; cross-connection programs require backflow assemblies to stop contamination.

options.a: Labeled by the manufacturer as suitable for plumbing
options.b: Accepted by the contractor based on past field experience
options.c: Listed/accepted for specific use by code or testing standard
options.d: Approved for any plumbing use once listed for one use

distractorExplanations.a: A manufacturer's own label is not approval; materials must be listed to a recognized standard and accepted by the AHJ.
distractorExplanations.b: Contractor preference is not code approval; the AHJ accepts materials listed to the referenced standards.
distractorExplanations.d: Listing is use-specific; a pipe listed for DWV service is not thereby approved for potable pressure service.

options.a: 1/2 inch (check local code table)
options.b: 3/4 inch (check local code table)
options.c: 1 inch nominal (check local code table)
options.d: 1-1/2 inches (check local code table)

distractorExplanations.a: 1/2 inch is a supply size; the code minimum vent is 1-1/4 in, and a bathroom group vent typically starts at 1-1/2 in.
distractorExplanations.b: 3/4 inch is below the code minimum vent diameter of 1-1/4 inches; vents that small choke and let trap seals siphon.
distractorExplanations.c: 1 inch is still under the 1-1/4 inch minimum vent size, so it cannot vent a bathroom group.

options.a: Fixture unit method and developed length/pressure available
options.b: Drainage fixture units and the slope of the building drain
options.c: Pipe velocity alone, ignoring friction loss over length
options.d: The meter size alone, matched to the main shutoff

distractorExplanations.b: DFUs and slope size the drainage system; supply piping uses water supply fixture units, length, and pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: Velocity limits matter, but sizing also accounts for friction loss over developed length and available pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: The meter is one input; branches are sized from fixture units, developed length, and the pressure available.

options.a: Connect to potable supply lines through a single check valve
options.b: Meet code for separation, filtration, and approved uses
options.c: Store untreated gray water for at least 72 hours
options.d: Include kitchen sink and toilet waste in the system

distractorExplanations.a: Gray water may not be cross-connected to potable piping; a single check valve is not acceptable protection.
distractorExplanations.c: Codes limit how long untreated gray water may be held (often 24 hours) to prevent odor and bacterial growth.
distractorExplanations.d: Toilet waste is blackwater and many codes exclude kitchen sinks; gray water comes from lavatories, showers, laundry.

options.a: Plan view of pipe routing drawn to scale from above
options.b: Elevation view of fixture heights on one wall only
options.c: 3D-like view of pipe routing for layout understanding
options.d: Cross-section of the building showing structural loads

distractorExplanations.a: Plan views show piping from above in two dimensions; isometrics draw runs at 30-degree angles to convey 3D routing.
distractorExplanations.b: Elevations show one face in 2D; an isometric shows the whole piping system in a single 3D-style view.
distractorExplanations.d: Structural sections are architectural or engineering sheets; isometric plumbing drawings depict pipe routing.

options.a: Electrical wiring for water heaters, pumps, and disposals
options.b: Structural framing and notching around plumbing penetrations
options.c: Utility rates charged for municipal water service
options.d: Plumbing in food establishments and public health facilities

distractorExplanations.a: Electrical wiring is enforced by the electrical inspector; health departments regulate sanitary plumbing in food sites.
distractorExplanations.b: Notching and boring limits are building-code structural issues; health departments oversee public health plumbing.
distractorExplanations.c: Rates are set by the utility or public service commission; health departments regulate sanitation and safe water.

options.a: Backflow preventers and plumbing devices
options.b: Fitting dimensions published in the B16 series
options.c: Model plumbing code text adopted by states
options.d: Fire sprinkler system installation rules

distractorExplanations.b: B16 fitting standards are published by ASME; ASSE standards focus on plumbing devices such as backflow preventers.
distractorExplanations.c: Model codes come from ICC (IPC) and IAPMO (UPC); ASSE writes performance standards for plumbing devices.
distractorExplanations.d: Sprinkler installation is covered by NFPA 13; ASSE covers backflow preventers and other plumbing device standards.

options.a: Apply to a single permit rather than the jurisdiction
options.b: Modify model code for regional conditions
options.c: Take effect without formal adoption by ordinance
options.d: Replace the model code with manufacturer instructions

distractorExplanations.a: Amendments are adopted by ordinance and apply jurisdiction-wide; a one-job deviation is a variance or modification.
distractorExplanations.c: Amendments must be formally adopted by the governing body; informal inspector preferences are not code amendments.
distractorExplanations.d: Manufacturer instructions apply through listings; amendments are jurisdiction-adopted edits to the model code.

options.a: 5 ft head of water or 3 psi air for 15 minutes with no drop
options.b: 10 ft head of water or 5 psi air for 5 minutes with no drop
options.c: 10 ft head of water or 5 psi air for 15 minutes with no drop
options.d: 100 psi water or 50 psi air for 15 minutes with no pressure drop

distractorExplanations.a: Values are too low; the DWV test is a 10 ft water head or 5 psi air held for 15 minutes without loss.
distractorExplanations.b: Duration is wrong: the head or air pressure must hold for 15 minutes, not 5, for the DWV test to pass.
distractorExplanations.d: Those are water-supply test pressures (IPC 312.5); DWV piping is tested with a 10 ft head or 5 psi air.
